Homogenization of Three Species Reaction Diffusion Equation in Perforated Domains

Saumyajit Das saumyajit.math.das@gmail.com Address: Department of Mathematics, Harish-Chandra Research Institute, A CI of Homi Bhabha National Institute, Chhatnag Road, Jhunsi, Allahabad 211 019, India.    Kshitij Sinha 23d0781@iitb.ac.in Address: Department of Mathematics, Indian Institute of Technology Bombay, Powai, Mumbai - 400076, Maharashtra, India.
Abstract

In this article we study the asymptotic behaviour of the solution of the three species chemical reaction-diffusion model with non-homogeneous Neumann boundary condition in a perforated domain. We investigate how the mass inflow at the microscale affects the three-species reaction–diffusion system at the macroscale. When the perforations vanish at a moderate rate, employing two-scale convergence we observe that the microscale effects are captured by a global source term in the homogenized equation, which remains a three-species reaction-diffusion system but with modified diffusion coefficients. However when the perforations vanish rapidly, the influence of the microscale mass inflow becomes negligible and the macroscopic limit remains the same reaction-diffusion system with the same diffusion coefficients.

1 Introduction

Reaction-diffusion equations describe a wide range of physical phenomenon including reversible chemical kinetics, gas combustion model, diffusion of pollutants into atmosphere or electro-deposition of Nickel-Iron alloy [27, 1, 19, 29]. The chemical reaction-diffusion equation governs the evolution (in time) of species concentration at various spatial locations in a reversible chemical kinetics with diffusion. The general chemical reaction-diffusion equation is associated with the following reversible chemical kinetics:

p1​X1+⋯+pm​Xm⇌k1k2q1​X1+⋯+qm​Xm,p_{1}X_{1}+\cdots+p_{m}X_{m}{\xrightleftharpoons[k_{1}]{k_{2}}}q_{1}X_{1}+\cdots+q_{m}X_{m},

where Xi\displaystyle X_{i} denotes the chemical species for 1≤i≤m\displaystyle 1\leq i\leq m, pi\displaystyle p_{i} and qi\displaystyle q_{i} denote the stoichiometric coefficients for 1≤i≤m\displaystyle 1\leq i\leq m and k1\displaystyle k_{1}, k2\displaystyle k_{2} represent the forward and backward reaction rates respectively. In this article, we are interested in the effect of homogenization of the three species chemical reaction diffusion equation governed by the following chemical kinetics

X1+X2⇋X3.X_{1}+X_{2}\leftrightharpoons X_{3}.

The mathematical model corresponding to the above reversible chemical kinetics is given by: for i=1,2\displaystyle i=1,2

{∂tai−di​Δ​ai=a3−a1​a2in​(0,T)×Ω∂ta3−d3​Δ​a3=a1​a2−a3in​(0,T)×Ω∇ai⋅n=∇a3⋅n=0on​(0,T)×∂Ωai​(0,x)=a0iin​Ωa3​(0,x)=a03in​Ω.\left\{\begin{aligned} \partial_{t}a^{i}-d_{i}\Delta a^{i}=&a^{3}-a^{1}a^{2}\qquad&&\text{in}\ (0,T)\times\Omega\\ \partial_{t}a^{3}-d_{3}\Delta a^{3}=&a^{1}a^{2}-a^{3}\qquad&&\text{in}\ (0,T)\times\Omega\\ \nabla a^{i}\cdot n=\nabla&a^{3}\cdot n=0\qquad&&\text{on}\ (0,T)\times\partial\Omega\\ a^{i}(0,x)=&a^{i}_{0}\qquad&&\text{in}\ \Omega\\ a^{3}(0,x)=&a^{3}_{0}\qquad&&\text{in}\ \Omega.\end{aligned}\right. (1.1)

The spatial domain is taken to be a bounded domain Ω⊂ℝ3\displaystyle\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{3} with C2+ν\displaystyle\mathrm{C}^{2+\nu} boundary with ν>0\displaystyle\nu>0. The unknowns a1,a2,a3:[0,T)×Ω→ℝ\displaystyle a^{1},a^{2},a^{3}:[0,T)\times\Omega\to\mathbb{R}, represent the concentrations of the three species X1,X2\displaystyle X_{1},X_{2} and X3\displaystyle X_{3} respectively. Furthermore, here n⁡(x)\displaystyle n(x) denotes the outward unit normal to Ω\displaystyle\Omega at the point x∈∂Ω\displaystyle x\in\partial\Omega. The initial data a01,a02\displaystyle a^{1}_{0},a^{2}_{0} and a03\displaystyle a^{3}_{0} are taken to be sufficiently smooth up to the closure of the domain and nonnegative. The diffusion coefficients d1,d2\displaystyle d_{1},d_{2} and d3\displaystyle d_{3} are taken to be strictly positive. This particular model has attracted a significant attraction in the mathematical community, particularly in the study of the global-in-time existence of solutions [27, 15] as well as in the analysis of the large time asymptotics of the solutions [14, 13].

In this article we analyze the effect of homogenization in the three species reaction-diffusion system. This model considers periodically distributed smooth holes inside the domain where mass flows from outside, enters the system and influences the reversible chemical kinetics. We also introduce a security zone near the boundary of the domain where no holes are present. A detailed description of the domain with periodically distributed holes (also called perforated domain) is provided in Section 1.1. Here the evolution (in time) of densities of chemical species X1,X2\displaystyle X_{1},X_{2} and X3\displaystyle X_{3} are captured by the following model:

where CI\displaystyle C^{I} is some positive constant, uniform in ε\displaystyle\varepsilon.

Observe that along the boundary of the holes, we have non-homogeneous Neumann data. Homogenization problems with non-homogeneous Neumann data, which are also closely related to the homogenization problems in porous media have attracted significant attraction in the mathematical community. We would like to refer the readers to [10, 11, 18, 21, 22] for various works on this topic.

Moreover, the source terms appearing on the right hand side of the system (1.2)-(1.4) are quadratic in nature, i.e., they are quadratic polynomials. Hence, our problem is also related to nonlinear quadratic parabolic homogenization problem. Similar systems are studied in [18, 17], where authors consider a fragmentation-coagulation model (a particular reaction-diffusion model with infinitely many unknowns), arising from biomedical research such as in the study of Alzheimer disease [18]. In [17] due to the dominance of coagulation the first source term remains bounded from above by zero which need not hold for the three species reaction-diffusion system given by (1.2)-(1.4). Motivated by the work in [17, 18], we study the effect of homogenization of the perforated domain to the system (1.2)-(1.4). While the authors consider a quadratic model in [17], due to the dominance of coagulation the first source term always remains bounded from above by zero. This property need not hold for the three species reaction-diffusion system, given by (1.2)-(1.4). Consequently, our approach for deriving various estimates differs significantly from theirs.

The homogenization problem in this case is to study the effective concentration of the species as the size of the perforations vanish. To study such an effect when the size of the perforations are of order of size ε\displaystyle\varepsilon, we employ the method of two-scale convergence which has been widely used to study the effect of perforated domains for different models (see [2, 17, 18, 26, 23, 24]). To apply two-scale convergence we need various uniform (in ε\displaystyle\varepsilon) estimates(see Section 2), after which passing to the limit as ε→0\displaystyle\varepsilon\to 0 gives us the effective concentrations. The effective concentrations satisfies similar equation but with an extra reaction rate. We will now introduce our main result.

Y∗=Y−T¯\displaystyle\displaystyle Y^{*}=Y-\overline{T} (1.11)

Ωδ:={x∈Ω:dist⁡(x,∂Ω)>δ}\Omega^{\delta}:=\{x\in\Omega:\dist{(x,\partial\Omega)}>\delta\} (1.12)

Rε\displaystyle R_{\varepsilon} :=⋃k∈ℐε(ε​k+ε⁡(Y∖σε​T¯))\displaystyle:=\bigcup_{k\in\mathcal{I}_{\varepsilon}}\big(\varepsilon k+\varepsilon(Y\setminus\sigma_{\varepsilon}\overline{T})\big)

1.2 Plan of the Paper

We divide this article in two sections and several appendices. In Section 2 we derive the uniform estimates which is required for the two-scale convergence in Lemma 2.1- Proposition 2.4. In Section 3, we give the prove the Theorem 1.1 using the two-scale convergence method. In Section 4, we derive the Theorem 1.3 by passing the limit using the compactness in L2\displaystyle\mathrm{L}^{2} for rapidly decaying hole. In Appendix A we derive the global-in-time existence of the solution to the system (1.2)-(1.4), and obtain regularity estimates. In Appendix B-D, we discuss various classical tools which are extensively used in our article such as the existence of extension operator in perforated domain, the trace inequality, Anisotropic Sobolev inequality and two scale convergence method. In the final Appendix E, we construct well-prepared initial data demonstrating that the homogenization of the model considered in this article can also be carried out for certain non-constant initial data. These initial datum are nonnegative, sufficiently smooth, satisfy the compatibility condition (1.5), uniform estimates as described in (1.6), and converge to smooth, nonnegative functions in the two-scale sense.

2 Uniform Estimates

We start with the following uniform (in ε\displaystyle\varepsilon) L2\displaystyle\mathrm{L}^{2}-integral estimate of the solution. It can be proved along a similar line as in [17, Lemma 2.1], [18]. The same estimate when there is no perforation in the domain can be found in [16]. Thus we omit the proof of the result.

Lemma 2.1.

Let aε1,aε2\displaystyle a^{1}_{\varepsilon},a^{2}_{\varepsilon} and aε3\displaystyle a^{3}_{\varepsilon} be the solution to the system (1.2)-(1.4). Then we have

‖aεi‖L2​((0,T),L2​(Ωrε))≤κ1,∀ 1≤i≤3,\|a^{i}_{\varepsilon}\|_{\mathrm{L}^{2}((0,T);\mathrm{L}^{2}(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}))}\leq\kappa_{1},\ \forall\,1\leq i\leq 3, (2.1)

where κ1\displaystyle\kappa_{1} is a positive constant, independent of ε\displaystyle\varepsilon.

We now move to establish similar uniform (in ε\displaystyle\varepsilon) L2\displaystyle\mathrm{L}^{2}-integral estimate of the gradient of the solution. We have the following lemma.

Lemma 2.2.

Proposition 2.3.

Let aε1,aε2\displaystyle a^{1}_{\varepsilon},a^{2}_{\varepsilon} and aε3\displaystyle a^{3}_{\varepsilon} be the solution to the system (1.2)-(1.4). Then we have

where we have used the following identity

+\displaystyle\displaystyle+ 2​d1​∫0s∫Ωrε(aε1)2​|∇aε1|2+2​∫0s∫Ωrε(aε1)4​aε2=2​∫0s∫Ωrε(aε1)3​aε3.\displaystyle\displaystyle 2d_{1}\int_{0}^{s}\int_{\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}}\big(a^{1}_{\varepsilon}\big)^{2}|\nabla a^{1}_{\varepsilon}|^{2}+2\int_{0}^{s}\int_{\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}}\big(a^{1}_{\varepsilon}\big)^{4}a^{2}_{\varepsilon}=2\int_{0}^{s}\int_{\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}}\big(a^{1}_{\varepsilon}\big)^{3}a^{3}_{\varepsilon}.

≤d1​‖ψ‖B​γ12​Ct​r12​κ212+d1​‖ψ‖B​γ12​Ct​r12​‖∇aε1​(s,⋅)‖L2​(Ωrε),\displaystyle\displaystyle\leq d_{1}\|\psi\|_{B}\gamma^{\frac{1}{2}}C_{tr}^{\frac{1}{2}}\kappa_{2}^{\frac{1}{2}}+d_{1}\|\psi\|_{B}\gamma^{\frac{1}{2}}C_{tr}^{\frac{1}{2}}\left\|\nabla a^{1}_{\varepsilon}(s,\cdot)\right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}})},

where the last step is due to Lemma 2.2 and (1.14). Thanks to Young’s inequality we obtain

𝒥1≤C12+d14​∫Ωrε|∇aε1​(s,⋅)|2,\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{1}\leq C_{12}+\frac{d_{1}}{4}\int_{\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}}\big|\nabla a^{1}_{\varepsilon}(s,\cdot)\big|^{2}, (2.24)

12​∫0s∫Ωrε(∂taε1)2+d14​∫Ωrε|∇aε1​(s,⋅)|2≤C10+C11+C12.\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{s}\int_{\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}}\big(\partial_{t}a^{1}_{\varepsilon}\big)^{2}+\frac{d_{1}}{4}\int_{\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}}|\nabla a^{1}_{\varepsilon}(s,\cdot)|^{2}\leq C_{10}+C_{11}+C_{12}.

Since the above inequality is true for a.e. 0≤s≤T\displaystyle 0\leq s\leq T, we get the desired result. Similar calculation holds true for aε2\displaystyle a^{2}_{\varepsilon} and aε3\displaystyle a^{3}_{\varepsilon}. ∎

4 Homogenization for 𝒪⁡(εα)\displaystyle\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{\alpha}) perforations

In this section, we homogenize the equation (1.2)-(1.4) for the case when the perforations are of the size 𝒪⁡(εα)\displaystyle\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{\alpha}) for α>1\displaystyle\alpha>1. Since all the bounds mentioned in Section 2 holds true for these perforations as well. We define the following function

𝔳εi​(t,x):=Eε​(aεi),\mathfrak{v}_{\varepsilon}^{i}(t,x):=E_{\varepsilon}(a_{\varepsilon}^{i}),

and from the calculations done in previous section we deduce that

𝔳εi→𝔳iin ​L2​((0,T),L2​(Ω)),\mathfrak{v}_{\varepsilon}^{i}\rightarrow\mathfrak{v}_{i}\qquad\text{in }\mathrm{L}^{2}((0,T);\mathrm{L}^{2}(\Omega)),

up to a subsequence, still indexed by ε\displaystyle\varepsilon. Also observe that in the current regime of the holes we have the following strong convergence

χΩrε→1,strongly in ​Lp​(Ω)​ for ​1≤p<∞.\displaystyle\displaystyle\chi_{\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}}\to 1,\ \text{strongly in }\mathrm{L}^{p}(\Omega)\text{ for }1\leq p<\infty.

aεi~→𝔳iin ​L2​((0,T),L2​(Ω)).\tilde{a_{\varepsilon}^{i}}\to\mathfrak{v}_{i}\qquad\text{in }\mathrm{L}^{2}((0,T);\mathrm{L}^{2}(\Omega)). (4.1)

Consider the boundary integral

Appendix A Existence Theory

In this section, we analyze the existence of global-in-time classical nonnegative solution to the three species reaction-diffusion system in the perforated domain Ωrε\displaystyle\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}.

Theorem A.1.

For i=1,2,3\displaystyle i=1,2,3, consider the system (1.2)-(1.4) with ε≪1\displaystyle\varepsilon\ll 1. Then there exists a unique global-in-time classical solution aεi\displaystyle a^{i}_{\varepsilon} to the system (1.2)-(1.4), satisfying

aεi∈W1,p​((0,T),Lp​(Ωrε))∩Lp​((0,T),W2,p​(Ωrε))∩L∞​((0,T)×Ωrε),a^{i}_{\varepsilon}\in\mathrm{W}^{1,p}((0,T);\mathrm{L}^{p}(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}))\cap\mathrm{L}^{p}((0,T);\mathrm{W}^{2,p}(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}))\cap\mathrm{L}^{\infty}((0,T)\times\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}),

for all i=1,2,3\displaystyle i=1,2,3, T∈(0,∞)\displaystyle T\in(0,\infty), and p∈(1,∞)\displaystyle p\in(1,\infty) with p≠32,3\displaystyle p\neq\frac{3}{2},3. Furthermore, the solution is interior smooth and

aεi≥0,∀i=1,2,3.a_{\varepsilon}^{i}\geq 0,\ \forall\,i=1,2,3.
Proof.

Combining the facts that

aε,0i∈W2,p​(Ωrε)andψ∈C1​([0,T],B),a_{\varepsilon,0}^{i}\in\mathrm{W}^{2,p}(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}})\quad\text{and}\quad\psi\in C^{1}([0,T],B),

where

B:=C1​(Ω¯,C#1​(Y))B:=C^{1}\big(\overline{\Omega};C^{1}_{\#}(Y)\big)

(with C#1​(Y)\displaystyle C^{1}_{\#}(Y) denoting the space of Y\displaystyle Y-periodic C1\displaystyle C^{1} functions), together with the compatibility condition (1.5), we conclude the desired result by following [27, Theorem 3.5] and [28, Theorem 1]. We would like to note that the nonnegativity of the solution comes from the quasipositive (A.1) structure of the source term (see [27, Lemma 1.1] for further details). ∎

For the convenience, we state below the result concerning the nonnegativity of the solution.

Lemma A.2 (Nonnegativity of solutions, [27]).

For 1≤i≤m\displaystyle 1\leq i\leq m, let μi>0\displaystyle\mu_{i}>0 be constant. Let ui:(0,T)×Ω→ℝ\displaystyle u_{i}:(0,T)\times\Omega\to\mathbb{R} be a classical solution of the system: for 1≤i≤m\displaystyle 1\leq i\leq m

{∂tui−μi​Δ​ui=fi​(u1,…,um)in ​(0,T)×Ω∇ui⋅n=β⁡(t,x)≥0on ​(0,T)×∂Ωui​(0,x)≥0in ​Ω.\left\{\begin{aligned} \partial_{t}u_{i}-\mu_{i}\Delta u_{i}&=f_{i}(u_{1},\dots,u_{m})&&\text{in }(0,T)\times\Omega\\ \nabla u_{i}\cdot n&=\beta(t,x)\geq 0&&\text{on }(0,T)\times\partial\Omega\\ u_{i}(0,x)&\geq 0&&\text{in }\Omega.\end{aligned}\right.

Assume that f=(f1,…,fm):ℝm→ℝm\displaystyle f=(f_{1},\dots,f_{m}):\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathbb{R}^{m} is quasipositive, that is,

fi(r1,…,ri−1,0,ri+1,…,rm)≥0,∀(r1,…,rm)∈[0,+∞)m.\displaystyle\displaystyle f_{i}(r_{1},\dots,r_{i-1},0,r_{i+1},\dots,r_{m})\geq 0,\quad\forall(r_{1},\dots,r_{m})\in[0,+\infty)^{m}. (A.1)

Then the solution remains nonnegative, namely ui≥0\displaystyle u_{i}\geq 0 for all 1≤i≤m\displaystyle 1\leq i\leq m.

Remark A.3.

It follows that both aεi\displaystyle a_{\varepsilon}^{i} and (aεi)2\displaystyle(a_{\varepsilon}^{i})^{2} admit L2\displaystyle\mathrm{L}^{2}-traces on the boundary ∂Ωrε\displaystyle\partial\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}. Moreover, the time derivative ∂taεi\displaystyle\partial_{t}a_{\varepsilon}^{i} also admits a boundary trace, which is understood in the sense of 𝒟′((0,T);W−1/2,2(∂Ωrε))\displaystyle\mathcal{D}^{\prime}\big((0,T);\mathrm{W}^{-1/2,2}(\partial\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}})\big). Hence all the regularity assumption we need for our analysis holds true.

Appendix B Extension Operator and its time derivative

In this section, we recall the existence of the following family of extension operators from [18, 10, 6] and construct the time derivative of these operators under certain scenarios.

Lemma B.1 (see [6, 10]).

There exists a family of linear continuous extension operators

Eε:H1​(Ωrε)→H1​(Ω)E_{\varepsilon}:\mathrm{H}^{1}(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}})\to\mathrm{H}^{1}(\Omega)

and a constant CE>0\displaystyle C_{E}>0, independent of ε\displaystyle\varepsilon, such that

Eε​v=vin ​Ωrε,E_{\varepsilon}v=v\quad\text{in }\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}},

and

‖Eε​v‖L2​(Ω)\displaystyle\|E_{\varepsilon}v\|_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\Omega)} ≤CE​‖v‖L2​(Ωrε),\displaystyle\leq C_{E}\|v\|_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}})},
∥∇Eεv∥L2​(Ω)\displaystyle\|\nabla E_{\varepsilon}v\|_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\Omega)} ≤CE​‖∇v‖L2​(Ωrε),\displaystyle\leq C_{E}\|\nabla v\|_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}})},

for each v∈H1​(Ωrε)\displaystyle v\in\mathrm{H}^{1}(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}).

Remark B.2.

If v∈L2​((0,T),H1​(Ωrε))\displaystyle v\in\mathrm{L}^{2}((0,T);\mathrm{H}^{1}(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}})) then Eε​v∈L2​((0,T),H1​(Ω))\displaystyle E_{\varepsilon}v\in\mathrm{L}^{2}((0,T);\mathrm{H}^{1}(\Omega)).

Using this extension operator we define a new operator as follows

𝒢ε:L2​(Ωrε)→L2​(Ω)\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon}:\mathrm{L}^{2}(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}})\to\mathrm{L}^{2}(\Omega)

such that

𝒢ε​ξ​(x)=limn→∞Eε​ϕn​(x),\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon}\xi(x)=\lim_{n\to\infty}E_{\varepsilon}\phi_{n}(x), (B.1)

where {ϕn}n≥1⊂H1​(Ωrε)\displaystyle\{\phi_{n}\}_{n\geq 1}\subset\mathrm{H}^{1}(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}) is such that

‖ϕn−ξ‖L2​(Ωrε)→0.\|\phi_{n}-\xi\|_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}})}\to 0.

Then we have the following Lemma for the operator 𝒢ε\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon}.

Lemma B.3.

𝒢ε\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon} as defined in (B.1) is a well-defined bounded linear operator such that for v∈L2​(Ωrε)\displaystyle v\in\mathrm{L}^{2}(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}})

𝒢ε​v=vin ​Ωrε,\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon}v=v\quad\text{in }\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}},

and

‖𝒢ε​v‖L2​(Ω)≤Cg​‖v‖L2​(Ωrε),\|\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon}v\|_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\Omega)}\leq C_{g}\|v\|_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}})},

where constant Cg>0\displaystyle C_{g}>0 is independent of ε\displaystyle\varepsilon. Furthermore for w∈H1​(Ωrε)\displaystyle w\in\mathrm{H}^{1}(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}})

𝒢ε​w=Eε​w.\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon}w=E_{\varepsilon}w. (B.2)

Using 𝒢ε\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon}, we define the time derivative of Eε\displaystyle E_{\varepsilon} in the following Theorem.

Theorem B.4.

Suppose u∈L2​((0,T),H1​(Ωrε))\displaystyle u\in\mathrm{L}^{2}((0,T);\mathrm{H}^{1}(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}})) and ∂tu∈L2​((0,T),L2​(Ωrε))\displaystyle\partial_{t}u\in\mathrm{L}^{2}((0,T);\mathrm{L}^{2}(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}})). Then Eε​u\displaystyle E_{\varepsilon}u is weakly differentiable with respect to time and it’s weak derivative is given by

∂tEε​u=𝒢ε​(∂tu).\partial_{t}E_{\varepsilon}u=\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon}(\partial_{t}u).

Furthermore ∂tEε​u∈L2​((0,T),L2​(Ω))\displaystyle\partial_{t}E_{\varepsilon}u\in\mathrm{L}^{2}((0,T);\mathrm{L}^{2}(\Omega)) and

‖∂tEε​u‖L2​((0,T),L2​(Ω))≤Cg​‖∂tu‖L2​((0,T),L2​(Ωrε)),\|\partial_{t}E_{\varepsilon}u\|_{\mathrm{L}^{2}((0,T);\mathrm{L}^{2}(\Omega))}\leq C_{g}\|\partial_{t}u\|_{\mathrm{L}^{2}((0,T);\mathrm{L}^{2}(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}))}, (B.3)

where constant Cg>0\displaystyle C_{g}>0 is as mentioned in Lemma B.3.

Proof.

Observe that u∈H1​((0,T),L2​(Ωrε))\displaystyle u\in\mathrm{H}^{1}((0,T);\mathrm{L}^{2}(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}})) and hence by [4, Proposition 9.3] we have

limh→0‖∂tu−u⁡(t+h,⋅)−u⁡(t,⋅)h‖L2​((δ,T−δ),L2​(Ωrε))=0,∀ 0<δ<T/4.\lim_{h\to 0}\left\|\partial_{t}u-\frac{u(t+h,\cdot)-u(t,\cdot)}{h}\right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{2}((\delta,T-\delta);\mathrm{L}^{2}(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}))}=0,\ \forall\,0<\delta<T/4. (B.4)

Let ϕ∈Cc∞​([t1,t2]×Ωrε)\displaystyle\phi\in\mathrm{C}_{c}^{\infty}([t_{1},t_{2}]\times\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}) be such that 0<t1<t2<T\displaystyle 0<t_{1}<t_{2}<T. Testing Eε​u\displaystyle E_{\varepsilon}u with ∂tϕ\displaystyle\partial_{t}\phi gives us

∫0T∫ΩEε​u⋅∂tϕ\displaystyle\displaystyle\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}E_{\varepsilon}u\cdot\partial_{t}\phi =limh→0∫t12T−(T−t22)∫ΩrεEε​u​ϕ⁡(t+h,⋅)−ϕ⁡(t,⋅)h\displaystyle\displaystyle=\lim_{h\to 0}\int_{\frac{t_{1}}{2}}^{T-(\frac{T-t_{2}}{2})}\int_{\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}}E_{\varepsilon}u\frac{\phi(t+h,\cdot)-\phi(t,\cdot)}{h}
=limh→0[∫t12+hT−(T−t22)+h∫ΩrεEε​u​(t−h,⋅)​ϕ​(t)h−∫t1T−(T−t22)∫ΩrεEε​u​(t,⋅)​ϕ​(t,⋅)h​𝑑x​𝑑t]\displaystyle\displaystyle=\lim_{h\to 0}\left[\int_{\frac{t_{1}}{2}+h}^{T-(\frac{T-t_{2}}{2})+h}\int_{\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}}\frac{E_{\varepsilon}u(t-h,\cdot)\phi(t)}{h}-\int_{t_{1}}^{T-(\frac{T-t_{2}}{2})}\int_{\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}}\frac{E_{\varepsilon}u(t,\cdot)\phi(t,\cdot)}{h}\,dxdt\right]
=limh→0∫t1t2∫ΩrεEε​u​(t−h,⋅)​ϕ​(t,⋅)−Eε​u​(t,⋅)​ϕ​(t,⋅)h\displaystyle\displaystyle=\lim_{h\to 0}\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\int_{\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}}\frac{E_{\varepsilon}u(t-h,\cdot)\phi(t,\cdot)-E_{\varepsilon}u(t,\cdot)\phi(t,\cdot)}{h}
=limh→0∫t1t2∫Ωrε𝒢ε​(u⁡(t−h,⋅)−u⁡(t,⋅)h)​ϕ​(t,⋅)\displaystyle\displaystyle=\lim_{h\to 0}\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\int_{\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}}\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon}\left(\frac{u(t-h,\cdot)-u(t,\cdot)}{h}\right)\phi(t,\cdot)
=∫t1t2∫Ωrε𝒢ε​(limh→0u⁡(t−h,⋅)−u⁡(t,⋅)h)​ϕ​(t,⋅)\displaystyle\displaystyle=\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\int_{\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}}\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon}\left(\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{u(t-h,\cdot)-u(t,\cdot)}{h}\right)\phi(t,\cdot)
=−∫t1t2∫Ω𝒢ε(∂u∂t)ϕ(t,⋅),\displaystyle\displaystyle=-\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\int_{\Omega}\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon}\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}\right)\phi(t,\cdot),

where we have used Dominated Convergence Theorem for first and fifth steps. Thus in the sense of distribution

∂tEε​(u)=𝒢ε​(∂tu).\partial_{t}E_{\varepsilon}(u)=\mathcal{G}_{\varepsilon}\left(\partial_{t}u\right).

Hence invoking Lemma B.3 yields inequality (B.3). ∎

Appendix C Trace Inequality and Anisotropic Sobolev Inequality

In this section, we recall the Trace inequality (see [3, 17, 18, 6, 5]) and the Anisotropic Sobolev Inequality (see [18, 17]).

Lemma C.1 (see [3, 6, 5]).

Let rε=𝒪⁡(ε)\displaystyle r_{\varepsilon}=\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon). Then there exists a constant Ct​r>0\displaystyle C_{tr}>0 which does not depend on ε\displaystyle\varepsilon, such that when v∈L​i​p​(Ωrε)\displaystyle v\in Lip(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}), then

‖v‖L2​(Γrε)2≤Ct​r​[1ε​∫Ωrε|v|2​𝑑x+ε​∫Ωrε|∇xv|2​𝑑x].\|v\|^{2}_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\Gamma_{r_{\varepsilon}})}\leq C_{tr}\left[\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\int_{\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}}|v|^{2}\,dx+\varepsilon\int_{\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}}|\nabla_{x}v|^{2}\,dx\right].

Let rε=𝒪⁡(εα)\displaystyle r_{\varepsilon}=\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{\alpha}) for α>1\displaystyle\alpha>1. Then there exists a constant Ct​r>0\displaystyle C_{tr}>0 which does not depend on ε\displaystyle\varepsilon, such that when v∈H1​(Ωrε)\displaystyle v\in\mathrm{H}^{1}(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}), then

∥v∥L2​(Γrε)2≤Ct​r{(rεε32)2​‖v‖H1​(Ωrε)21<α≤3,rε​‖v‖H1​(Ωrε)2α>3.\|v\|^{2}_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\Gamma_{r_{\varepsilon}})}\leq C_{tr}\left\{\begin{aligned} &\left(\frac{r_{\varepsilon}}{\varepsilon^{\frac{3}{2}}}\right)^{2}\|v\|^{2}_{\mathrm{H}^{1}(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}})}\qquad 1<\alpha\leq 3,\\ &r_{\varepsilon}\|v\|^{2}_{\mathrm{H}^{1}(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}})}\qquad\alpha>3.\end{aligned}\right.
Lemma C.3 (Anisotropic Sobolev inequalities in perforated domains, see [18]).
  • (i).

    For q1\displaystyle q_{1} and r1\displaystyle r_{1} satisfying the conditions

    {1r1+32​q1=34,r1∈[2,∞],q1∈[2,6],\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{r_{1}}+\dfrac{3}{2q_{1}}=\dfrac{3}{4},\\[10.0pt] r_{1}\in[2,\infty],\ q_{1}\in[2,6],\end{cases} (C.1)

    the following estimate holds (\displaystyle(for OPENv∈H1​((0,T),L2​(Ωrε))∩L2​((0,T),H1​(Ωrε))):\displaystyle v\in\mathrm{H}^{1}((0,T);L^{2}(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}))\cap L^{2}((0,T);\mathrm{H}^{1}(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}))):

    ‖v‖Lr1​((0,T),Lq1​(Ωrε))≤CA​S​‖v‖Qrε​(T),\|v\|_{L^{r_{1}}((0,T);L^{q_{1}}(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}))}\leq C_{AS}\|v\|_{Q_{r_{\varepsilon}}(T)}, (C.2)

    ‖v‖Qrε​(T)2:=sup0≤t≤T∫Ωrε|v⁡(t)|2​𝑑x+∫0Td​t​∫Ωrε|∇v​(t)|2​𝑑x.\|v\|_{Q_{r_{\varepsilon}}(T)}^{2}:=\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\int_{\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}}|v(t)|^{2}\,dx+\int_{0}^{T}dt\int_{\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}}|\nabla v(t)|^{2}\,dx. (C.3)

Proof of Anisotropic Sobolev Inequality depends upon the existence of Extension operator which exists thanks to Appendix B. Hence we get that Anisotropic Sobolev Inequality holds true for the case when α>1\displaystyle\alpha>1.

Appendix D Two-Scale Convergence

In this section, we gather some useful results on two-scale convergence (see [2, 3, 25, 24, 9, 20])

Definition D.1 (see [2]).

A sequence of functions vε\displaystyle v^{\varepsilon} in L2​((0,T),L2​(Ω))\displaystyle\mathrm{L}^{2}((0,T);\mathrm{L}^{2}(\Omega)) two-scale converges to v0∈L2​((0,T),L2​(Ω×Y))\displaystyle v_{0}\in\mathrm{L}^{2}((0,T);\mathrm{L}^{2}(\Omega\times Y)) if

limε→0∫0T∫Ωvε​(t,x)​ϕ​(t,x,xε)​𝑑t​𝑑x=∫0T∫Ω∫Yv0​(t,x,y)​ϕ​(t,x,y)​𝑑t​𝑑x​𝑑y\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}v^{\varepsilon}(t,x)\,\phi\left(t,x,\frac{x}{\varepsilon}\right)dt\,dx=\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}\int_{Y}v_{0}(t,x,y)\,\phi(t,x,y)\,dt\,dx\,dy

for all ϕ∈C1​([0,T]×Ω¯,C#∞​(Y))\displaystyle\phi\in C^{1}([0,T]\times\overline{\Omega};C^{\infty}_{\#}(Y)).

We recall the following classical Proposition:

Proposition D.2.

If vε\displaystyle v^{\varepsilon} is a bounded sequence in L2​((0,T)×Ω)\displaystyle L^{2}((0,T)\times\Omega), then there exists a function v0:=v0​(t,x,y)\displaystyle v_{0}:=v_{0}(t,x,y) in L2​((0,T)×Ω×Y)\displaystyle L^{2}((0,T)\times\Omega\times Y) such that, up to a subsequence, vε\displaystyle v^{\varepsilon} two-scale converges to v0\displaystyle v_{0}.

Then, the following Proposition is useful for obtaining the limit of the product of two two-scale convergent sequences.

Proposition D.3.

Let vε\displaystyle v^{\varepsilon} be a sequence of functions in L2​((0,T)×Ω)\displaystyle L^{2}((0,T)\times\Omega) which two-scale converges to a limit v0∈L2​((0,T)×Ω×Y)\displaystyle v_{0}\in L^{2}((0,T)\times\Omega\times Y). Suppose furthermore that

limε→0∫0T∫Ω|vε​(t,x)|2​𝑑t​𝑑x=∫0T∫Ω∫Y|v0​(t,x,y)|2​𝑑t​𝑑x​𝑑y.\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}|v^{\varepsilon}(t,x)|^{2}\,dt\,dx=\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}\int_{Y}|v_{0}(t,x,y)|^{2}\,dt\,dx\,dy.

Then, for any sequence wε\displaystyle w^{\varepsilon} in L2​((0,T)×Ω)\displaystyle L^{2}((0,T)\times\Omega) that two-scale converges to a limit w0∈L2​((0,T)×Ω×Y)\displaystyle w_{0}\in L^{2}((0,T)\times\Omega\times Y), we get the limit

limε→0∫0T∫Ωvε​(t,x)​wε​(t,x)\displaystyle\displaystyle\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}v^{\varepsilon}(t,x)\,w^{\varepsilon}(t,x) ϕ⁡(t,x,xε)​d​t​d​x\displaystyle\displaystyle\,\phi\left(t,x,\frac{x}{\varepsilon}\right)dt\,dx
=∫0T∫Ω∫Yv0​(t,x,y)​w0​(t,x,y)​ϕ​(t,x,y)​𝑑t​𝑑x​𝑑y,\displaystyle\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}\int_{Y}v_{0}(t,x,y)\,w_{0}(t,x,y)\,\phi(t,x,y)\,dt\,dx\,dy,

for all ϕ∈C1​([0,T]×Ω¯,C#∞​(Y))\displaystyle\phi\in C^{1}([0,T]\times\overline{\Omega};C^{\infty}_{\#}(Y)).

The next Propositions yield a characterization of the two-scale limits of gradients of bounded sequences vε\displaystyle v^{\varepsilon}. This result is crucial for applications to homogenization problems.

Proposition D.4.

Let vε\displaystyle v^{\varepsilon} be a bounded sequence in L2​((0,T),H1​(Ω))\displaystyle L^{2}((0,T);\mathrm{H}^{1}(\Omega)) that converges weakly to a limit v:=v⁡(t,x)\displaystyle v:=v(t,x) in L2​((0,T),H1​(Ω))\displaystyle L^{2}((0,T);\mathrm{H}^{1}(\Omega)). Then, vε\displaystyle v^{\varepsilon} also two-scale converges to v\displaystyle v, and there exists a function v1:=v1​(t,x,y)\displaystyle v_{1}:=v_{1}(t,x,y) in L2​((0,T)×Ω,H#1​(Y)/ℝ)\displaystyle L^{2}((0,T)\times\Omega;\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\#}(Y)/\mathbb{R}) such that, up to extraction of a subsequence, ∇vε\displaystyle\nabla v^{\varepsilon} two-scale converges to ∇xv​(t,x)+∇yv1​(t,x,y)\displaystyle\nabla_{x}v(t,x)+\nabla_{y}v_{1}(t,x,y).

The main result of two-scale convergence can be generalized to the case of sequences defined in L2​([0,T]×Γε)\displaystyle L^{2}([0,T]\times\Gamma_{\varepsilon}).

Proposition D.5 (see [2, 3]).

Let vε\displaystyle v^{\varepsilon} be a sequence in L2​((0,T)×Γε)\displaystyle L^{2}((0,T)\times\Gamma_{\varepsilon}) such that

ε​∫0T∫Γε|vε​(t,x)|2​𝑑t​d​σε​(x)≤C\varepsilon\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Gamma_{\varepsilon}}|v^{\varepsilon}(t,x)|^{2}\,dt\,d\sigma_{\varepsilon}(x)\leq C (D.1)

where C\displaystyle C is a positive constant, independent of ε\displaystyle\varepsilon. There exist a subsequence (still denoted by ε\displaystyle\varepsilon) and a two-scale limit v0​(t,x,y)∈L2​((0,T)×Ω,L2​(Γ))\displaystyle v_{0}(t,x,y)\in L^{2}((0,T)\times\Omega;L^{2}(\Gamma)) such that vε​(t,x)\displaystyle v^{\varepsilon}(t,x) two-scale converges to v0​(t,x,y)\displaystyle v_{0}(t,x,y) in the sense that

limε→0ε​∫0T∫Γεvε​(t,x)​ϕ​(t,x,xε)​𝑑t​d​σε​(x)=∫0T∫Ω∫Γv0​(t,x,y)​ϕ​(t,x,y)​𝑑t​𝑑x​𝑑σ​(y)\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\varepsilon\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Gamma_{\varepsilon}}v^{\varepsilon}(t,x)\,\phi\left(t,x,\frac{x}{\varepsilon}\right)dt\,d\sigma_{\varepsilon}(x)=\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}\int_{\Gamma}v_{0}(t,x,y)\,\phi(t,x,y)\,dt\,dx\,d\sigma(y) (D.2)

for any function ϕ∈C1​([0,T]×Ω¯,C#∞​(Y))\displaystyle\phi\in C^{1}([0,T]\times\overline{\Omega};C^{\infty}_{\#}(Y)).

Appendix E Well-prepared Initial Condition

Our analysis is based on the fact that the solution remains nonnegative throughout the time and space. Furthermore, the initial condition should satisfy the compatibility condition as described in (1.5) and the uniform (in ε\displaystyle\varepsilon) estimates as described in (1.6). To ensure the solutions remains nonnegative, we consider positive initial condition satisfying the compatibility condition (1.5). Then the quasipositive (A.1) structure of the source term along with the positive Neumann boundary condition will ensure that our solution remains nonnegative throughout the time [27, Lemma 1.1]. In this section, we focus on selecting the nonnegative initial condition for each domain Ωrε\displaystyle\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}, satisfying the compatibility condition (1.5) and the uniform estimates (1.6). For i=1,2,3\displaystyle i=1,2,3, consider smooth functions a0i:Ω¯→(0,∞)\displaystyle a_{0}^{i}:\overline{\Omega}\to(0,\infty) such that

∇a0i⋅n=0at∂Ω,i=1,2,3.\nabla a_{0}^{i}\cdot n=0\ \text{at}\ \partial\Omega,\ i=1,2,3.

Hence there exists a constant ℐm​i​n>0\displaystyle\mathcal{I}_{min}>0 such that

ξa0i(x)≥ℐm​i​n,∀x∈Ωand∀i=1,2,3,\displaystyle\displaystyle\xi a_{0}^{i}(x)\geq\mathcal{I}_{min},\ \ \forall x\in\Omega\ \text{and}\ \forall\,i=1,2,3, (E.1)

where ξ=|Y∗|−1\displaystyle\xi=|Y^{*}|^{-1}, where |Y∗|\displaystyle|Y^{*}| denotes the measure of the portion of the unit cube outside the hole, as defined in (1.11).

Next we construct a well prepared initial condition from the smooth functions a0i\displaystyle a_{0}^{i} for i=1,2,3\displaystyle i=1,2,3. We construct our initial conditions for periodically distributed spherical hole. It can be generalized to any type of holes with smooth boundary.

Let rε=ε\displaystyle r_{\varepsilon}=\mathcal{\varepsilon}. Fix an ε\displaystyle\varepsilon-cell inside Ωrε\displaystyle\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}} and let the spherical hole inside it is centered at xk\displaystyle x_{k} with radius rε<ε4\displaystyle r_{\varepsilon}<\frac{\varepsilon}{4}, which is strictly contained inside Ω\displaystyle\Omega. Let k∈ℐε\displaystyle k\in\mathcal{I}_{\varepsilon}, where #​ℐε\displaystyle\#\mathcal{I}_{\varepsilon} denotes the number of holes at each ε\displaystyle\varepsilon-scale (recall (1.13)). Consider the following equation: for i=1,2,3\displaystyle i=1,2,3

{−Δ​wk,εi=0,in​B​(xk,2​rε)∖B⁡(xk,rε)¯∇wik,ε⋅n=−ξ∇ai0⋅non​∂B⁡(xk,rε)wk,εi=0on​∂B⁡(xk,2​rε).\left\{\begin{aligned} -\Delta w^{i}_{k,\varepsilon}=&0,\qquad&&\text{in}\ B(x_{k},2r_{\varepsilon})\setminus\overline{B(x_{k},r_{\varepsilon})}\\ \nabla w^{i}_{k,\varepsilon}\cdot n=&-\xi\nabla a^{i}_{0}\cdot n\qquad&&\text{on}\ \partial B(x_{k},r_{\varepsilon})\\ w_{k,\varepsilon}^{i}=&0\qquad&&\text{on}\ \partial B(x_{k},2r_{\varepsilon}).\end{aligned}\right. {∫B⁡(xk,2​rε)∖B⁡(xk,rε)¯|wk,εi|2​dx≤C3​rε5,∫B⁡(xk,2​rε)∖B⁡(xk,rε)¯|∇xwk,εi|2​dx≤C3​rε3.\left\{\begin{aligned} \int\limits_{B(x_{k},2r_{\varepsilon})\setminus\overline{B(x_{k},r_{\varepsilon})}}|w^{i}_{k,\varepsilon}|^{2}\,dx\leq&C_{3}r^{5}_{\varepsilon},\\ \int\limits_{B(x_{k},2r_{\varepsilon})\setminus\overline{B(x_{k},r_{\varepsilon})}}|\nabla_{x}w^{i}_{k,\varepsilon}|^{2}\,dx\leq&C_{3}r^{3}_{\varepsilon}.\end{aligned}\right. (E.13)

Summing them over all holes, we obtain

{∑k∈ℐε∫B⁡(xk,2​rε)∖B⁡(xk,rε)¯|wk,εi|2​dx≤C3​rε5​#​ℐε,∑k∈ℐε∫B⁡(xk,2​rε)∖B⁡(xk,rε)¯|∇xwk,εi|2​dx≤C3​rε3​#​ℐε.\left\{\begin{aligned} \sum_{k\in\mathcal{I}_{\varepsilon}}\int\limits_{B(x_{k},2r_{\varepsilon})\setminus\overline{B(x_{k},r_{\varepsilon})}}|w^{i}_{k,\varepsilon}|^{2}\,dx\leq&C_{3}r^{5}_{\varepsilon}\#\mathcal{I}_{\varepsilon},\\ \sum_{k\in\mathcal{I}_{\varepsilon}}\int\limits_{B(x_{k},2r_{\varepsilon})\setminus\overline{B(x_{k},r_{\varepsilon})}}|\nabla_{x}w^{i}_{k,\varepsilon}|^{2}\,dx\leq&C_{3}r^{3}_{\varepsilon}\#\mathcal{I}_{\varepsilon}.\end{aligned}\right. (E.14)

We use the fact that rε3​#​ℐε≤γ1\displaystyle r^{3}_{\varepsilon}\#\mathcal{I}_{\varepsilon}\leq\gamma_{1} (1.14). Furthermore, thanks to the fact that the support of each wk,εi\displaystyle w^{i}_{k,\varepsilon} is disjoint (for a fixed i\displaystyle i) and they can be extended as H1\displaystyle\mathrm{H}^{1} functions outside B⁡(xk,2​rε)\displaystyle B(x_{k},2r_{\varepsilon}) by zero, we have that

{‖∑k∈ℐεw^k,εi‖L2​(Ωrε)2≤C3​γ1​rε2,‖∑k∈ℐεw^k,εi‖H1​(Ωrε)2≤C3​γ1,\left\{\begin{aligned} \left\|\sum_{k\in\mathcal{I}_{\varepsilon}}\hat{w}^{i}_{k,\varepsilon}\right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}})}^{2}\leq&C_{3}\gamma_{1}r^{2}_{\varepsilon},\\ \left\|\sum_{k\in\mathcal{I}_{\varepsilon}}\hat{w}^{i}_{k,\varepsilon}\right\|_{\mathrm{H}^{1}(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}})}^{2}\leq&C_{3}\gamma_{1},\end{aligned}\right. (E.15)

where w^k,εi\displaystyle\hat{w}^{i}_{k,\varepsilon} is the extension of wk,εi\displaystyle w^{i}_{k,\varepsilon} by zero beyond B⁡(xk,2​rε)\displaystyle B(x_{k},2r_{\varepsilon}). We use the following Sobolev embedding

‖f‖L4​(Λ0)≤Cs​o​b​‖f‖H1​(Λ0),∀f∈H1​(Λ0),Cs​o​b>0,\|f\|_{\mathrm{L}^{4}(\Lambda_{0})}\leq C_{sob}\|f\|_{\mathrm{H}^{1}(\Lambda_{0})},\ \forall\,f\in\mathrm{H}^{1}(\Lambda_{0}),\ C_{sob}>0,

in (E.12). It yields

Again, change of variable x↔xk+rε​y\displaystyle x\leftrightarrow x_{k}+r_{\varepsilon}y yields

‖wk,εi‖L4​(B⁡(xk,2​rε)∖B⁡(xk,rε)¯)4≤C32​Cs​o​b2​rε7.\|w^{i}_{k,\varepsilon}\|_{\mathrm{L}^{4}\left(B(x_{k},2r_{\varepsilon})\setminus\overline{B(x_{k},r_{\varepsilon})}\right)}^{4}\leq C_{3}^{2}C_{sob}^{2}r^{7}_{\varepsilon}.

Using the fact that the support of the functions wk,εi\displaystyle w^{i}_{k,\varepsilon} are disjoint (for a fixed i\displaystyle i), we have that

where γ1\displaystyle\gamma_{1} is as defined in (1.14). Choice of the constant CW:=max⁡{C3​γ1,C3​Cs​o​b​γ114}\displaystyle C_{W}:=\max\{\sqrt{C_{3}\gamma_{1}},\sqrt{C_{3}C_{sob}}\gamma_{1}^{\frac{1}{4}}\}, yields our result. ∎

The above L2\displaystyle\mathrm{L}^{2} integral estimate helps us to obtain two-scale limit (see Appendix D) of the well prepared initial data aε,0i\displaystyle a^{i}_{\varepsilon,0}, for each i=1,2,3\displaystyle i=1,2,3.

Lemma E.4.

For i=1,2,3\displaystyle i=1,2,3, consider the well prepared initial condition aε,0i\displaystyle a^{i}_{\varepsilon,0} as described in (E.4). Then, as ε→0\displaystyle\varepsilon\to 0, the two-scale limit (\displaystyle(see Appendix D)\displaystyle) is given by

aε,0i⇀2​-scaleξ​a0i​χY∗.a^{i}_{\varepsilon,0}\xrightharpoonup{2\text{-scale}}\xi a_{0}^{i}\chi_{Y^{*}}.
Proof.

Thanks to Lemma E.3, we have that

‖∑k∈ℐεw^k,εi‖L2​(Ωrε)→0,as​ε→0.\left\|\sum_{k\in\mathcal{I}_{\varepsilon}}\hat{w}^{i}_{k,\varepsilon}\right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}})}\to 0,\ \text{as}\ \varepsilon\to 0.

Hence, the 2-scale limit of ∑k∈ℐεw^k,εi\displaystyle\displaystyle{\sum_{k\in\mathcal{I}_{\varepsilon}}\hat{w}^{i}_{k,\varepsilon}} is 0\displaystyle 0. Furthermore, since

α​a0i​χΩrε⇀2−s​c​a​l​eξ​a0i​χY∗,\alpha a^{i}_{0}\chi_{\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}}\xrightharpoonup{2-scale}\xi a_{0}^{i}\chi_{Y^{*}},

we conclude our result. ∎

Remark E.5.

When rε=𝒪⁡(εα)\displaystyle r_{\varepsilon}=\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{\alpha}) and α>1\displaystyle\alpha>1 we observe that

χΩrε→1​ strongly in ​L2​(Ω).\chi_{\Omega_{r_{\varepsilon}}}\to 1\text{ strongly in }\mathrm{L}^{2}(\Omega).

Hence a similar construction as done for the case of rε=𝒪⁡(ε)\displaystyle r_{\varepsilon}=\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon), will produce a sequence of initial data {aε,0i}ε\displaystyle\{a^{i}_{\varepsilon,0}\}_{\varepsilon} which strongly converges to a0i\displaystyle a^{i}_{0} in L2​(Ω)\displaystyle\mathrm{L}^{2}(\Omega) and satisfies the compatibility condition (1.5) and the uniform estimates (1.6).
